name: Drum synthesis and hybrid percussion (kick, snare, clap, hats, taiko, epic hits)
goal: Synthesize a complete kit and cinematic percussion from oscillators and noise: kick pitch envelope, snare body + noise, 3-burst clap, hats, toms/taiko from noise with resonant filters, layered epic hybrid hits, ensemble multiplication, resampled velocity layers, and drive to cut through.

sources.title: EPIC Cinematic Drums from White Noise | A Sound Design Tutorial
Crazy Percussions Out of a Pad in Serum 2
Ableton Sound Design Tutorial - Drums That Cut Through The Mix
How to Make Your Own Epic Hybrid Drums WITHOUT Buying New Sounds (Tutorial)
The VITAL Drum Sound Design Tutorial!! (FREE PLUGIN)

theory: Drums are short envelopes on simple sources: kick = sine with fast pitch drop; snare = tuned body + noise; clap = repeated noise bursts; hats = high-passed noise. Layering + micro-timing (0-22 ms) creates ensemble size.
prerequisites: A DAW piano roll for programming the capture notes
A DAW that can duplicate tracks and MIDI
A DAW to render and test the sounds in a beat
A parallel bus or split-lane routing
A sampler or drum sampler that can auto-record input into layers, with velocity split and round-robin modes, a velocity-modulated filter and humanize/random start
A synth drum patch (epic hybrid / ensemble drum skills)
A synth or host with macros, per-note random modulation and a tempo-synced step-sequencer LFO
A synth with several oscillators, noise sources, pitch and filter envelopes with adjustable curve, distortion and filters
A synth with sine/saw oscillators, white noise, drawable envelopes or multi-stage LFOs in envelope mode, two filters and basic FX
A synthesized drum hit (noise + oscillator with fast pitch/filter envelopes) or a tom sample
A synthesized drum patch (noise/oscillator hit with amp and filter envelopes; see the epic hybrid drum skill)

outputs.name: result
outputs.description: Rendered part or recipe following the workflow

constraints: Portable recipe; not affiliated with any vendor; do not copy factory presets or sample packs.
Numbers in variants come from the source video transcripts; workflow steps are the consolidated mainstream practice.
Bring drums in early and avoid pitch wobble unless asked (user preferences from daily tests).

steps.action: Kick: sine, pitch env 150 -> 45 Hz in ~35 ms, amp decay 200-400 ms, short click/noise transient; HP ~20 Hz, notch boxiness ~78 Hz if needed.
Snare: two sines (~180/330 Hz) + band-passed noise 1.5-9 kHz, decay 60-150 ms.
Clap: three noise bursts ~10 ms apart + tail, band 1-6 kHz; hats: noise HP >7 kHz, closed 20-40 ms, open 200-300 ms.
Toms/taiko: noise or sine through resonant HP/BP, velocity -> decay and filter, soft-clip + hall.
Epic hit: 4 parallel layers with pitch drops (+5/+29 st), noise burst, curved fast envelopes; distant boom = tom + sub + 6 dB LP + big reverb low-cut 100 Hz.
Ensemble: duplicate hits 4x with random 0-22 ms delays, ±40 pan, varied decay; resample to 8 velocity layers / round robins to avoid machine-gun.
Cut-through: band-pass a copy, overdrive it, blend parallel level-matched.
steps.expect: Drums audible in a dense mix

steps.action: Hear the theory: run `/home/box/audio-tools/bin/python sample-lab/theory/drums_synthesis.py` from the repo root and compare the sections; reuse its functions as a starting point for renders.
steps.expect: WAV in sample-lab/theory/out/ demonstrating the principle

verification: Render a short test and A/B against a reference at matched loudness
Run the generator and confirm it writes a WAV without error
Check mono compatibility and that no element masks the kick/bass

variants.name: Cinematic taiko-style ensemble drums from white noise: velocity sets the amp and filter decay, a resonant 60 Hz high-pass plus low boost adds weight, a tanh soft clip and limiter go before a large-hall convolution reverb, with optional detuned sine, FM sub and round-robin sample layers
variants.goal: Make big cinematic ensemble drums (taiko-like) with no recordings, using any synth with a noise oscillator, a filter, two envelopes and velocity sensitivity. Think in four categories: frequency, amplitude, time and timbre. Start with white noise; amp envelope with no sustain and a short decay, with velocity routed to decay (soft hits short, hard hits long and ringing) and a wide velocity-to-level range. Add a low-pass filter (about 1 kHz) with its own short envelope on cutoff, also scaled by velocity, so each hit starts bright and closes darker; add a little filter drive. EQ: resonant high-pass at about 60 Hz plus a low bell boost for weight, a mud cut, presence, a slight high shelf; add a little release so hits breathe. Soft clip (tanh waveshaper) driven a little by that low boost to mimic an overloaded ensemble, trim the output and the extreme sub. Put a limiter or maximizer, then a convolution reverb with a cathedral or large-hall impulse (shortened, low end tamed, highs damped, about 5 kHz lifted). Layers: several detuned sines with a pitch envelope for tone, an FM sub at 20-50 Hz, and a round-robin layer of rattly found-object hits with slight random pitch to avoid machine-gunning.
steps: Load white noise in a fresh patch; set the amp envelope to sustain 0 and a short decay; widen the velocity-to-level range.
Route velocity to amp decay so soft hits are short and hard hits ring out long.
Add a low-pass (about 1 kHz) and a second envelope on cutoff with a short decay, opening bright at the attack and closing darker; scale its amount or decay by velocity and add a little filter drive.
EQ for weight: resonant high-pass at about 60 Hz plus a low bell boost; cut mud, add some presence and a slight high shelf; add a little amp release.
Soft clip with a tanh waveshaper (small drive), trim the output, filter a little extreme sub.
Add a limiter, THEN a convolution reverb with a cathedral or large-hall impulse; shorten the decay, tame the low end, damp the highs and lift about 5 kHz.
Optional layers: 3 detuned sines with a pitch-drop envelope (tone), an FM or sine sub at 20-50 Hz, and a round-robin layer of found-object or rattle hits with slight random pitch.

variants.name: Turn a synth tom-style epic drum hit into a distant low explosion / drop boom: harmonic bass enhance plus an octave-down sub, a 6 dB/oct low-pass instead of an attack boost, reverb low-cut around 100 Hz at 24 dB/oct, a band-limited quarter-note delay with about 7 ms early/late L/R offsets, a parallel tremolo or auto-pan tail whose depth is faded in by a delayed envelope, and an optional low comb filter (about 14-40 Hz) for a modern metallic drop
variants.goal: Make a far-away 'whoa, what happened' cinematic boom for drops and section hits, starting from a synthesized drum hit (see the epic hybrid drum / taiko-from-noise skills for building the hit itself). This skill adds the distance, sub and tail processing: a rumbling, darker boom with a moving stereo tail.
steps: Play the hit lower on the keyboard so it sounds less like a tom. Reshape the body with filter-envelope decay, cutoff, resonance and noise amount.
Add harmonic bass enhancement plus a sub oscillator one octave down (two octaves only if needed). Move the low-cut EQ from about 83 Hz down to about 50 Hz and steepen it from 24 to 36 dB/oct.
Remove any attack/snap boost band and replace it with a gentle 6 dB/oct low-pass.
Reverb: low-cut the reverb itself at about 100 Hz with a 24 dB/oct slope (by ear), choose a large impulse and set the mix to about 40%.

Optional: add a tempo-synced quarter-note delay with resonance off, high-pass the delay at about 90 Hz and low-pass it at about 4 kHz, and lower its level. Offset the left repeat about 7.3 ms early and the right about 7.3 ms late.

Optional parallel tail: split the signal after the reverb into a parallel lane with a tremolo (rectangle, eighth notes, depth up, blend about 50%). Drive the tremolo depth with an envelope: delay about 140 ms, decay about 2 s (match the reverb length), sustain 0.
Alternative tail: replace the tremolo with a quarter-note auto-pan using the same envelope on depth, or put distortion or other modulation on the parallel lane.

Optional modern 'deep metal' drop: add a comb filter on the lane, tuned low, about 14-40 Hz (12 Hz is too low), with feedback about 50% and max frequency reduced to tame the highs. Blend it with the split ratio, and you can add the delay after it.

variants.name: Turn a flat sustained drone into rolling shaker-style percussion: loop and crossfade a stable bar, re-envelope it into rhythmic hits with a transient-preserving time-stretch gate at a fast note rate, then low-cut, boost one tuned mid harmonic, layer an organic shaker texture, snap it with a transient shaper and add a short parallel bright room
variants.goal: Recycle a pad/drone into tuned percussion without a drum source. Pick the steadiest, least peaky bar of the drone, loop it with short crossfades to avoid clicks, consolidate, then use a transient-preserving warp/stretch mode with a fast transient rate (the presenter starts at a 1/60-type rate for shaker speed) and reduce the per-transient sustain/envelope so each grid step becomes a hit. Add a fade-in, consolidate again, high-pass the lows, boost the strongest mid harmonic so the hit is in key (the presenter's was G#), layer a shaker/tambourine texture (less hold, more attack, a little decay, slight pitch, denser), add a transient shaper (attack up, sustain way down), tidy with EQ and finish with a short, bright, no-pre-delay room in parallel (~22 ms, mixed under the dry).
steps: Find the most stable, least peaky bar of the drone and loop it. Crossfade at each loop join so there are no clicks, then consolidate to one file.

Set a transient-preserving stretch mode with linear behaviour, choose a fast transient rate for shaker speed, then reduce the transient sustain/envelope until each step becomes a short hit. Raise level, add a small fade-in, and consolidate again.
EQ: high-pass the low frequencies that are not part of the percussion, then boost one or two mid harmonics so the part has a pitch that fits the tune or groove.

Layer an organic texture (tambourine/shaker-type) with less hold, more attack, a little more decay, slight pitch shift and higher density. EQ the texture to fill what is not poking through and reduce its decay.
Add a transient shaper: raise attack, remove a lot of sustain, adjust speed so it is snappy but not overdone.
Final EQ: bring up the gap left by processing, roll off extremes, and let the main harmonic breathe.
Put a very short bright room (no pre-delay, little depth, ~22 ms) on a parallel chain beside the dry signal and mix it under.

variants.name: Make a weak drum (e.g. a clap) cut through and drive the groove with band-passed overdrive: choose the band that gets distorted, push the drive too far then back off, use tone to tame harsh top, set the dynamics control low for a tight punch, blend dry/wet, and level-match
variants.goal: Fix a drum hit that sounds wimpy or sits on top of the mix. On the soloed hit (reverb off, low cut kept so it doesn't fight the kick and bass), insert an overdrive with a band-pass before the distortion stage, inside a group with a gain utility after it for level matching. Sweep the band-pass to find the range you want to emphasize (avoid the thick, murky lows) and narrow the Q roughly. Push the drive hard to hear what it does, then back it off (about 60%) so the brittle upper-mid hiss doesn't dominate. Use the tone control as a top-end cut. Set the dynamics control lower for a tighter, punchier, shorter-feeling hit, or higher for a washed-out, relaxed one (it acts like note length and articulation for the groove). Dial dry/wet (parallel) from about 50 to 100%. Level-match against bypass with the gain utility, then put the reverb back and fine-tune in context, leaving final tweaks for the mixdown.
steps: Solo the hit, bypass its reverb, keep its low-cut EQ.
Insert band-pass -> overdrive -> gain utility in a group.
Add a little drive and sweep the band-pass centre to find the range to emphasize; avoid murky lows; narrow the Q roughly.
Push the drive too far to hear the effect, then back off (about 60%) until the brittle top isn't dominant; lower the tone to cut harsh upper mids if needed.
Set the dynamics control low (about 20-30) for tight punch, or higher for a looser, washed-out feel.
Set dry/wet (50-100%) in context with the full mix.
Level-match with the utility against bypass, restore the reverb (adjust decay), and leave final tweaks to the mixdown.

variants.name: Epic trailer-style hybrid drum built from a four-layer synth hit (pitched additive and FM oscillators with very fast exponential pitch drops, e.g. +5 and +29 semitones, plus filtered white and pink noise bursts with overload, tube drive, MS-20-style low-pass and a high-pass) layered with any three acoustic drum samples including bleed/ambient mics, then glued with a scooped EQ, sub trim, multiband compression and gentle upward (OTT-style) compression
variants.goal: Make big hybrid drums from tools you already have. Synth drum (one patch, four channels): (1) a simple additive/harmonic oscillator, stereo, with a pitch envelope dropping from about 5 semitones up, plus white noise through a low-pass whose cutoff envelope closes extremely fast with a strong exponential curve (a pitched, roto-tom-like burst); (2) pink noise through an aggressive low-pass with the same envelope, then a second overloaded filter that also takes channel 1's signal for grit; (3) an FM (or simple triangle/square) oscillator with a very fast pitch drop into tube distortion, an MS-20-style low-pass and a high-pass to remove rumble; (4) another additive high-content oscillator whose pitch drop starts about 29 semitones up, giving parallel pitch drops with channel 1. Key: very fast, strongly curved envelopes that hit hard and decay to nothing; play lower or higher on the keyboard for pitch, or several notes for a flam/ensemble. Global: two EQs, compression and reverb. Acoustic layer: any three acoustic drum samples, mixed with room/bleed mics (snare, hats, toms, ambience) so the kick is not dead. Process the combined layers: heavily scooped EQ for a trailer sound, trim the very lowest subs, per-layer EQ (less top on acoustic), multiband compression on the low end letting transients through, and optionally OTT-style compression at low depth with more upward than downward. Render the acoustic element, set its notes to the sample's root pitch and add the same fast envelope in the sampler; add velocity tracking for dynamics.
steps: Channel 1: additive/harmonic oscillator, stereo, with a pitch envelope dropping from about +5 semitones; fast exponential amp envelope.
Channel 2: white noise into a low-pass whose cutoff envelope closes extremely fast with a strong curve.
Channel 3: pink noise into an aggressive low-pass using the same envelope, then a second overloaded filter that also receives channel 1.
Channel 3: FM (or triangle/square) oscillator with a very fast pitch drop into tube distortion, an MS-20-style low-pass, then a high-pass to cut rumble.
Channel 4: a second additive high-content oscillator whose pitch drop starts about +29 semitones; play with channel 1 for parallel pitch drops.
Add global EQ (two), compression and reverb; compare a less-curved envelope to confirm the strong curve is needed.
Layer three acoustic drum samples, bringing up bleed/ambient mics (snare, hats, toms, room) so the low drum has life.
On the combined layers: heavily scooped EQ, trim the very lowest subs, per-layer EQ (e.g. less top on the acoustic), multiband compression on the low band letting transients through.
Optionally add OTT-style compression at low depth with more upward than downward; EQ after any extreme multiband effect.
Render the acoustic element, set its notes to the sample's root pitch, apply the same fast envelope in the sampler and add velocity tracking to both layers.

variants.name: Resample a synthesized epic drum into a reusable sampler instrument: record 8 spaced hits on a velocity ramp into auto velocity-split layers (soften the velocity-to-amp curve so the softest layer is still audible), or record 8 slightly different hits as round-robins for fast repeats (16ths/32nds without machine-gunning), add velocity-to-low-pass (floor about 1-1.5 kHz) and small start-time jitter, and bounce a panned 4-5 instance ensemble as its own multisample
variants.goal: Stop running several synth instances for one drum. Capture the epic drum (see the synth drum ensemble skill for the multi-instance setup) into a sampler with velocity layers or round-robins, so it can be reused across songs, played in fast rolls, and loaded into a Web Audio sample player for Polyrhythm Studio.
steps: Set the sampler to record its input (external/aux input) with auto-advance to the next layer per hit. Turn off per-instance random envelope delay on the synth for a single-instance capture.
Program 8 capture notes spaced far enough apart to decay fully (no dense 16ths), alternating a little for variation. For velocity mode, scale the velocities as a ramp from low (not too low) to high.
Arm and play. For velocity mode, set the layer mode to auto velocity-split and reduce the velocity-to-amplitude amount so the softest layer is still audible.
For repeated hits or rolls, instead record 8 hits at slightly different velocities (and random settings) and set the layer mode to round-robin.

Add velocity to low-pass cutoff (floor about 1-1.5 kHz, harder hits open it) so soft hits sound softer even in round-robin mode. Optionally add start-time (pre-delay) jitter, a little under about 9 ms.

Ensemble bounce: copy the MIDI to 4-5 synth instances with different pan (about 85 L/R and 46 L/R), randomness, pitch offset, snap frequency, decay and velocity curve. Sum them to one bus and capture that bus into the sampler the same way.
Save the instrument with a clear name, for example 'big tom drum synth'.

variants.name: Make one synth epic-drum patch sound like an ensemble of drummers: copy it to about four instances on the same MIDI, give each a different global decay, snap-EQ frequency and pan (about ±40), and add per-note random envelope delay (about 0-22 ms, tighten to about 7 ms, too loose at 65 ms) so the hits flam naturally. Optionally drive a filter with a tempo-synced step sequencer for rhythmic patterns
variants.goal: Layer synthesized epic drums into a big, human-feeling ensemble quickly. Copying the same patch and MIDI usually just sounds like one louder hit. Put a few macro controls on the patch (global decay, snap frequency, global pitch, timing randomness) so each copy differs with a few slider moves, instead of editing each synth and the MIDI by hand.
steps: Add macros to the patch: global decay (amp-env and filter-env decay together), snap frequency (a peaking EQ band on the attack), global pitch in semitones (about ±4) and randomness depth.

Add a per-note random modulator (new value on every MIDI note) on the amp-envelope delay and filter-envelope delay. Range about 0-22 ms at 50% randomness; 100% gives about 0-65 ms (too loose), and about 9% gives about 7 ms (tight).
Write a simple pattern on instance 1, then duplicate the instance and its MIDI about three times.
On each copy, move the macros differently: decay up or down, snap frequency up or down, randomness slightly different, small fixed pitch offset. Pan pairs about 39-40 left and right.
Listen and tighten: if a layer is too loose, lower its randomness (for example 86 to 68, 90 to 60).

Optional rhythmic variant: an arpeggiator on eighth notes or a tempo-synced step-sequencer LFO driving the filter cutoff range. Change the step pattern or rate (8 to 16 steps, double speed) for new grooves. Lengthen the attack to turn hits into reverse-drum or noise-sweep textures.

variants.name: Synthesize a whole drum kit (808, kick, clap, snare, closed and open hat) from a basic synth: sine and noise sources, envelope-drawn transients, fast pitch envelopes, and targeted EQ, then test and re-tweak each sound inside a real beat
variants.goal: Build six drum sounds in one synth with no samples. 808: sine tuned so its fundamental sits around 45 Hz (an octave below where it first lands), plus a saw and white noise whose levels follow a drawn envelope with a quick dip for the transient; low-pass the saw; boost mids a little, soft-clip, use a very gentle high-pass around 20 Hz (a steep one sounds bad), and a narrow bell cut around 78 Hz; optional parallel copy with reverb faded in and kept to the sides. Kick: sine pitched down, very short amp envelope, a very fast pitch envelope (about 0.07 s) on pitch, soft clip, light bit-crush, multiband drive, cut boxy mids around 400 Hz, high-pass. Clap: white noise whose level envelope has three quick transients then one longer decay (about 0.085 s spacing on a 9-step grid), band-limited (energy above about 600 Hz, key areas about 1 kHz and 6 kHz), high end added with bells not shelves, a little chorus and very short delays for width, compression, reduce side highs. Snare: two or three sines in octaves (the reference showed tones at about 240, 484 and 1 kHz), noise with two quick transients, one shared filter, a very short pitch envelope on all tones, distortion; optionally layer the clap. Closed hat: white noise, about 0.22 s envelope, band/high-pass that keeps some mids. Open hat: longer noise envelope with a second transient, low-cut reverb, very short (1/64) ping-pong delay, shorten decay to taste. Render each and tweak inside a beat (e.g. re-export pitched up a few semitones).
steps: 808: sine osc tuned so the fundamental reads about 45 Hz on an analyser; add a saw and white noise whose levels follow a drawn envelope (quick dip at the start for a transient, then decay, about 1.6 s overall); low-pass the saw.

808 processing: small mid boost, soft distortion with modest drive, very gentle high-pass near 20 Hz (not steep), narrow bell cut around 78 Hz; optional parallel copy with reverb faded in, kept to the sides, then a limiter on the pair.

Kick: sine pitched down an octave, very short amp envelope, a very fast envelope (about 0.07 s) routed to pitch, soft clip; then light bit-crush, multiband drive, a cut around 400 Hz for boxiness and a high-pass.

Clap: white noise with a level envelope of three quick transients then one longer decay (grid of about 9 steps, about 0.085 s); band-pass it so energy sits above about 600 Hz with emphasis near 1 kHz and 6 kHz; add highs with bells not shelves and avoid much content above about 11 kHz.
Clap finishing: a little chorus and very short delays for stereo, compression, then turn down side highs.

Snare: two or three sines an octave apart (reference tones about 240 Hz, 484 Hz, 1 kHz), white noise with two quick transients, all through one filter; route a very short envelope to the pitch of every tone; add distortion; optionally layer the clap and blend.

Closed hat: white noise with a very short envelope (about 0.22 s), filter to a tick, high-pass but keep some mids. Open hat: same noise, longer envelope with a second small transient, low-cut reverb and a 1/64 ping-pong delay, then shorten the decay.
Render all pieces, build a short beat, and adjust each sound in context (EQ, decay, pitch shift a few semitones and re-export) until they sit together.
